title: Drift Harp
pitch: A harp of plucked strings that you strum by dragging a finger or cursor across them, each string a physically modelled Karplus-Strong string tuned in pure just intonation on a live 3-by-5 lattice. Play a looping chord progression and hear and see the pitch creep up by a syntonic comma (about a fifth of a semitone) every lap, a trick called a comma pump. A tempering dial lets you squeeze the drift shut and hear exactly what equal temperament trades away.
whyNow: Timeless: a tuning-system explorer where the surprise is audible. The visitor discovers on their own that pure intervals do not close a loop, which most explainers only state in words.

research.summary: A comma pump is a repeating progression whose pure intervals almost, but not exactly, return to the start, so the pitch shifts by a tiny interval each lap. The standard case is the syntonic comma (81:80, roughly 21.5 cents) in the progression C G D A E C. A 5-limit just intonation lattice puts fifths (3/2) on one axis and major thirds (5/4) on the other, and a loop around the lattice that does not close is the drift made visible. Karplus-Strong gives a cheap plucked string: a short noise burst circulating in a filtered delay line, where loop length sets pitch and the in-loop averaging filter sets decay and brightness. That fits an AudioWorklet or a ScriptProcessor-free delay-buffer implementation with several voices. Browser Karplus-Strong instruments exist, which de-risks the sound engine, but none found combines it with a drifting lattice.

sources.title: Comma pump
sources.snippet: Describes a comma pump as a sequence, often chords, that shifts pitch by a small interval each repetition; the usual example is C G D A E C raising pitch by 81:80 in just intonation.
sources.note: Defines the drift mechanic and the 81:80 example

sources.title: Comma pump (Xenharmonic Wiki)
sources.snippet: Independent wiki entry covering comma pumps: loops of just intervals that nearly close, tempered out in systems that equate the comma to unison.
sources.note: Second independent description of comma pumps

sources.title: Just Intonation: pitch drift explanation (FIU)
sources.snippet: University page explaining that in just intonation one note name can have several pitches a syntonic comma (about 21.5 cents) apart, and that choirs meet this as drift.
sources.note: Source for the roughly 21.5 cent size and real-world drift

sources.title: Karplus-Strong string synthesis
sources.snippet: Physical-modelling method: a burst of noise recirculates through a filtered delay line; loop length sets pitch, filter sets decay. Invented by Alexander Strong and analysed by Kevin Karplus.

sources.title: Karplus Strong Algorithm (CCRMA, Stanford)
sources.snippet: Stanford physical audio signal processing text on the Karplus-Strong algorithm, a delay line with a lowpass in the feedback loop.

sources.title: Lattice (music)
sources.snippet: Pitch lattices place just ratios on axes by prime; the 5-limit lattice uses 3/2 and 5/4, drawn as square or hexagonal grids; the gap between a 5/4 third and the Pythagorean third is the syntonic comma.

sources.title: karplus stress tester (GitHub)
sources.snippet: A browser project that plucks virtual Karplus-Strong strings as a custom audio processing exercise; notes glitches when the browser cannot keep up.
sources.note: Shows the string engine runs in browsers; also a performance warning

facts.claim: A comma pump is a progression that returns almost, but not exactly, to its starting pitch, shifting by a small interval each repetition; the classic syntonic example is C G D A E C, rising by 81:80 per lap in just intonation (as described on Wikipedia and the Xenharmonic Wiki).
In just intonation one note name can sound at pitches separated by a syntonic comma, about 21.5 cents, as reported on a university just-intonation page (one result).
Karplus-Strong synthesis recirculates a noise burst through a filtered delay line; delay length sets pitch and the loop filter shapes decay and tone.
As of 2026-10-12, per a search result for the Lattice (music) article, 5-limit lattices put 3/2 and 5/4 on the two axes; this was seen in one result only and is unconfirmed here.

inspirations: pitch lattice diagrams from xenharmonic tuning software

design.coreLoop: Drag across strings to strum, assemble a short loop of chords on the lattice, and let it cycle. Each lap the drift meter shows the pure tuning rising by one syntonic comma while a ghost of the starting pitch stays put. Turn the tempering dial to close the loop and hear what is lost, or chase a lap that lands back home using adaptive retuning. Every chord choice changes how fast and which way the pitch wanders, so there is always another loop to try.
sophisticationHooks: Karplus-Strong voices with per-string damping, pick position and a stroke-speed-dependent excitation, polyphonic across a harp of 12 to 24 strings
Live 5-limit pitch lattice with ratio and cents readouts; the drift is the distance between where a loop starts and where it ends on the lattice
Tempering dial that continuously morphs pure ratios toward 12-tone equal temperament, with a seeded generative drone that makes beating audible
Shareable URL hash holding the chord loop, tempering amount and seed
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: one AudioWorklet or delay-buffer string engine with voice pool, canvas harp and lattice views, pointer/touch strum and keyboard play, loop editor with 8 slots, drift meter, tempering dial, about panel. Cut: MIDI export, 7-limit and higher primes, recording, presets beyond four.
risks: AudioWorklet from a blob or inline module may be blocked by the page CSP, so a delay-buffer fallback in the main audio graph is needed
Audio only starts after a user gesture and cannot be verified by a headless screenshot, so visuals must carry the story when muted
Lattice view as seen in one search result only; the page cites it as a general method, not a dated fact
